payload.stem: An economy's production possibilities curve is bowed outward (concave to the origin). Which of the following is true?

options.text: There is no opportunity cost of moving along the curve.
options.why: Believes there is no trade-off along the curve; every movement along a PPC gives up some of the other good.

options.text: The economy can produce any combination outside the curve if it trades.
options.why: Confuses trade (consumption beyond the PPC) with the production possibilities themselves.

options.text: The opportunity cost of producing more of one good is constant at every output level.
options.why: Describes a straight-line PPC, not a bowed-out one.

options.text: The opportunity cost of producing more of one good increases as more of that good is produced.
options.why: A bowed-out PPC shows increasing opportunity costs because resources are not equally suited to both goods.

options.text: Resources are perfectly adaptable to the production of either good.
options.why: Perfectly adaptable resources would give a straight line, not a bowed-out curve.

payload.stem: The table shows the hours of labor each country needs to produce one unit of chairs or one unit of tables. Which country should specialize in producing chairs to gain from trade?

stimulus.description: Hours of labor needed to produce one unit of each good.

options.text: Country A, because it needs more hours to produce each good.
options.why: Treats a larger labor requirement as an advantage; it indicates lower productivity.

options.text: Both countries should produce chairs because each can produce it.
options.why: Ignores that gains from trade come from specialization based on different opportunity costs.

options.text: Country B, because it gives up fewer units of tables to produce a unit of chairs.
options.why: The opportunity cost of one unit of chairs is 2/2 = 1.00 units of tables in Country A and 1/2 = 0.50 in Country B.

options.text: Country A, because it gives up fewer units of tables to produce a unit of chairs.
options.why: Reverses the opportunity-cost comparison.

options.text: The country that needs fewer hours per unit of chairs, regardless of what it gives up of tables.
options.why: Uses an absolute advantage (fewer hours) rather than a comparative advantage (lower opportunity cost).

options.text: Changing the required reserve ratio to alter the money multiplier.
options.why: The money multiplier and reserve requirement are the main tools only in an economy with limited reserves.

payload.stem: Which of the following is true of the long-run Phillips curve (LRPC)?

options.text: It is downward sloping, so policymakers can permanently lower unemployment by accepting higher inflation.
options.why: Describes the short-run trade-off as if it were permanent.

options.text: It is upward sloping because inflation raises unemployment in the long run.
options.why: Describes stagflation in the short run, not the long-run curve.

A decrease in nominal wages in a recession. is incorrect: Falling nominal wages shift SRAS in the long-run adjustment; potential output is unchanged.
A temporary decrease in the price of oil. is incorrect: A temporary cost change shifts SRAS but not LRAS.
An increase in the price level caused by higher aggregate demand. is incorrect: A price-level change moves the economy along SRAS; it does not shift LRAS.
An increase in government purchases. is incorrect: A change in government purchases shifts AD, not LRAS.

key_scoring.notes: Option A is the only cause of a permanent rightward LRAS shift. B shifts SRAS, C is temporary and shifts SRAS, D is a movement along the curves, and E shifts AD.

The correct answer is Exports become more expensive to foreigners and imports become cheaper, so net exports fall and aggregate demand shifts to the left.. Net exports are a component of aggregate demand.
Net exports do not change, because exchange rates affect only financial assets. is incorrect: Exchange rates affect the prices of traded goods.
Exports and imports both rise, so aggregate demand is unchanged. is incorrect: An appreciation changes relative prices in opposite directions for exports and imports.
Exports become cheaper to foreigners and imports become more expensive, so net exports rise and aggregate demand shifts to the right. is incorrect: Reverses the effect of an appreciation on relative prices.
Aggregate supply shifts to the left, so real GDP falls. is incorrect: The main short-run effect works through aggregate demand.

scope_skill.notes: Topic 6.5: currency appreciation, net exports and aggregate demand. The task is a two-step causal chain (relative prices to net exports to AD to real GDP), which fits skill 2.B.

key_scoring.notes: A is the unique defensible answer. B, C and D are clearly wrong. E is wrong because appreciation does not shift short-run aggregate supply.

stimulus_expression.notes: No stimulus is needed. The stem is clear and has the five options (A-E) required for AP Macroeconomics.

distractor_explanation.notes: The 'why' texts for the options are weak or mismatched. Option A's 'why' is a generic statement, not an explanation of the key. Option B's 'why' ('Exchange rates affect the prices of traded goods') is acceptable. Option E's 'why' ('main short-run effect works through aggregate demand') is a weak rebuttal that never says AS does not shift. Option C's 'why' is vague, and C is internally odd because it says both exports and imports rise. The explanation text has a doubled period and is formulaic, so it does not clearly explain each wrong option or the misconception it encodes.

exam_suitability.notes: Short reading load and about 60 seconds. The calculator designation is harmless. The stem is a bit generic, but it is typical of an AP item.

review.summary: The item is content-correct, with a unique key and appropriate scope. It fails on distractor quality and explanation.
